$comment: FROZEN held-out evaluation set for kgf agent/domain selection.
Authored 2026-09-13 against library_version 29.97.4, BEFORE any ranker
existed in kgf. That ordering is the point: a set written or adjusted after
tuning measures curve-fitting, not accuracy. Do not add, remove or relabel
a case to make a ranker look better. If a label is genuinely wrong, fix it
in a commit that changes NO ranker code, and say why.
Labels are sets of acceptable domains, not single answers, because several
of these tasks legitimately sit on a boundary (a slow query is arguably
backend or database work). A case with one acceptable domain is a case where
any other answer is wrong.
Three categories, chosen to include the classes that fail today:
proper-noun  - names a framework or product. The easy class, and the only
one the existing reference implementation reliably gets
right: dropping 'spring boot' from a task moved it from
spring-boot-microservices to figma-automation-engineer.
plain-english- no proper noun at all. The class that fails today.
no-description- the best skill is one of the 134 skills with NO description,
where a lexical ranker has only name + domain to weigh. This
is the trigger condition for revisiting the no-embeddings
decision, so it has to be measurable.

provenance.method: 33 cases authored by hand before the ranker was tuned, labelled by acceptable_domains rather than by a single expected answer. Raw task text scored with Selector(graph, library). Engineered text produced 2026-09-14 by the real production path -- engineer_context then engineer_prompt, groq/qwen3.6-27b via the reasoner role -- and frozen here so the floor is calibrated against the text production actually ranks.

$comment: Measured 2026-09-12 against claude-workflow-engine's selection/ package
at library_version 29.97.4, using load_catalogue + build_lexicon +
DomainKgAdapter + RiskSignal.unavailable(), complexity=8, limit=3.
Recorded because it is the bar kgf must beat, and because neither figure
was re-derived during plan review -- so its provenance is pinned here
rather than quoted from memory. 8 tasks, 4 correct top-1 domains.
The confidence pair is the justification for the calibration criterion:
a wrong answer scored 0.776 while a correct one scored 0.835. Those
populations overlap, so a low_confidence state keyed on score alone could
never fire.
Measured 2026-09-13 at library_version 29.97.4. Recorded here so the
figure has provenance rather than living in a commit message.
HONEST CAVEAT: the ranker was developed with this set visible, so 54.5%
is optimistic for unseen tasks. What guards against having simply fitted
33 cases is that no label was changed, no per-case rule exists, and each
design decision was made on a diagnosed mechanism -- the one change that
mattered most was fixing an ordering bug, and the one plausible-sounding
addition (a coverage factor on the agent score) was MEASURED, found to
hurt, and reverted.
Three scoring designs were compared -- enriched agent documents,
skills-primary aggregation, and skills-primary plus a domain signal -- and
all three landed within a few points of each other while plain-english
stayed at 3-4 of 15. The ceiling is a property of this corpus, not of the
formula: the vocabulary that separates domains ('endpoint', 'repository',
'cache') is spread across many domains' skill text.
The no-description category was PREDICTED to be the hardest and is now
the second strongest, because all 134 of those skills do have a markdown
description that the registry build dropped. Reading the markdown fixed a
class that embeddings were being reserved for.
Re-measured 2026-09-14 at library_version 29.98.0, on the ENGINEERED
prompt -- which is what orchestrator.py ranks. The previous record was
taken on RAW task text and got two of the three wrong (#38).
Trigger 1 (top-3 below 75% or top-1 below 50%): FIRES.
top-3 66.7%, top-1 54.5%. Only the top-3 half fires; top-1 is above
its bar. Engineering the prompt IMPROVED top-3 (60.6% -> 66.7%) and
left top-1 unchanged at 18/33.
Trigger 2 (>=3 misses among description-less skills): FIRES at 4.
The previous record said False, citing '6 of 8 correct' -- true of
RAW text, where only 2 missed. On engineered text 4 miss. This is a
correction, not a regression in the ranker.
Trigger 3 (>=3 misses where disambiguation edges were consulted and
still lost): WITHDRAWN AS VACUOUS.
Derived properly from SelectionResult.disambiguation_considered, now
that M7 made the field exist: the edges are consulted on 33 of 33
cases (list sizes 7..24, mean 14.4), so the condition is
arithmetically identical to '>=3 misses' and restates trigger 1. It
cannot distinguish the abap-rap-engineer-for-Postgres class it was
written to detect. The previous record justified it with a PROXY --
'11 of 15 plain-english cases' -- which is not what M11 defines.
Keeping it would make the gate look like three independent signals
when it has two.
DECISION: embeddings are TRIGGERED, on 1 and 2, which fire on real and
independent grounds. Implementing them carries an accepted dependency
cost and is tracked separately.

Develop a Solidity smart contract implementing a two-party escrow mechanism. The contract must accept a deposit from an initiator, hold the funds securely, and require explicit confirmation from both the initiator and a designated counterparty before releasing the funds. Upon mutual confirmation, the funds must be transferred back to the original depositor. You must implement state variables to track the confirmation status of each party individually. Implement strict access control so that only the respective party can call the function to confirm their side. Emit events for all state-changing actions, including deposits, confirmations, and fund releases, to ensure transparency.

Adhere to the following specific constraints:
1. Use Solidity version 0.8.0 or higher.
2. Include checks-effects-interactions patterns to prevent reentrancy attacks.
3. Validate that the deposit amount is greater than zero.
4. Ensure that a party cannot confirm more than once.
5. Prevent any withdrawal attempts until both confirmation flags are true.

Handle the following edge cases explicitly:
1. Reject transactions where the deposit value is zero.
2. Revert if a party attempts to confirm after they have already confirmed.
3. Revert if a withdrawal is attempted before both parties have confirmed.
4. Ensure funds remain locked if only one party has confirmed.

Output the complete, compilable Solidity code for the contract. Include necessary comments explaining the state variables and the logic flow. Do not include any external library imports unless they are standard OpenZeppelin contracts for security primitives if deemed necessary, but prefer native Solidity implementations for simplicity unless specific security features require otherwise.

CRITICAL CONSTRAINT: The contract MUST strictly enforce that funds are only released when BOTH parties have explicitly confirmed; no partial releases or unilateral withdrawals are permitted under any circumstances.

$comment: Issue #16. The floor was calibrated on RAW task text while
production ranks the ENGINEERED prompt. Both distributions are
measured here on the same 33 cases.
THE HEADLINE: the previous floor of 0.45 admitted 33 of 33
engineered cases, because the minimum engineered confidence is
0.4758. A threshold meant to withhold weak matches never fired in
production, and reported all 15 wrong top-1 answers as 'selected'.
HONEST CAVEAT, twice over. The floor was chosen on the same 33
cases it is scored against, so its 0.750 precision is optimistic
for unseen tasks. And the Clopper-Pearson 95% interval
[0.476, 0.927] has a lower bound BELOW the 0.545 admit-everything
base rate -- so at n=33 the precision gain is not statistically
established. What is established is that 0.45 did nothing.

calibration.interval: Clopper-Pearson 95%, exact rather than Wald: n=33 near p=0.5 is where Wald misreports
